title: Being Tired Changes What You See
author: Leadership Insights
summary: This Leadership essay argues that fatigue does not simply make people sloppier at handling situations, it actively distorts the situation being perceived before any reasoning even begins. Using a recurring example of a terse end-of-day email that reads as hostile at 6pm and neutral the next morning, the author distinguishes fatigue's effect from ordinary output degradation: the input itself, not just the response to it, has already been altered by tiredness. The piece extends this to rushing and chronic stress, arguing that time pressure causes people to stop gathering information early and mistake an incomplete picture for a complete one, while chronic stress causes ambiguous events to be read as adversarial over and over in a pattern too gradual to notice day to day. Because none of these states announce themselves, tiredness feels like 'the world being more annoying,' not like an internal condition, the essay argues the only reliable countermeasure is procedural: hold a conclusion reached while tired, rushed, or stressed until it survives a second look in a different state before acting on it. The piece closes by returning to its opening example to show how a single night's sleep silently reversed the reading of an identical two-line email.
points: Distinguishes fatigue's effect on perception (the situation itself looks more hostile) from its effect on output quality (being merely sloppier), arguing the former is the more dangerous and less visible failure mode.

Argues rushing causes people to stop gathering information early while feeling they have gathered enough, producing 'a complete picture that happened to come together fast' rather than a visibly incomplete one.

Notes that chronic stress causes ambiguous events to be repeatedly read as adversarial, a pattern that is hard to detect because it lacks the clear before/after contrast a single bad night's sleep provides.
Recommends a procedural fix rather than a willpower fix: hold high-stakes conclusions reached while tired or stressed until they survive a second look in a rested state before acting on them.
quotes: When you're tired, the email is more hostile, the problem is less solvable, the person across the table is less reasonable. You're not misreading something clear.

When you're tired, you stop producing alternatives. The first interpretation that shows up is the one you go with, because building a second one is work and there's nothing left in the tank to build it with.
Everybody understands that rushing makes you decide faster. What gets missed is that it also makes you decide on less.
Under stress the ambiguous thing gets read as adversarial, and it gets read that way over and over.
Tired doesn't feel like an altered condition. It feels like the world being more annoying than usual.
Being tired doesn't make your read wrong. Plenty of tired reads turn out to be correct. What it does is lower how much that read has earned your trust.
